summary: PIM-SM is a multicast routing protocol that can use the existing unicast routing table or a separate multicast one. It builds one-way shared trees rooted at a Rendezvous Point for each group, and can optionally switch to shortest-path trees. This revised specification updates the earlier PIM-SM documents.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 7761 specifies Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM), the routing protocol that carries one copy of a multicast stream across a network to many receivers. It is called protocol independent because it can take its topology information from the ordinary unicast routing table without depending on any particular routing protocol. This matters because PIM-SM is the Internet Standard specification routers implement to deliver multicast groups across wide-area networks.

subtitle: How routers deliver multicast traffic to groups of receivers by meeting at a Rendezvous Point and then optionally taking shortcuts.

tldr.problem: Multicast traffic has to get from sources to receivers across wide-area networks, even though neither side knows the other exists in advance.
tldr.mechanism: Receivers' routers send Join messages hop by hop towards a Rendezvous Point (RP) for the group, building a shared tree. Senders' routers register with the RP, and routers can then optionally switch to a shortest-path tree for each source.
tldr.outcome: RFC 7761 is an Internet Standard (STD 83) that replaces RFC 4601, is meant to interoperate with it, and drops a few features that lacked deployment experience.

today: RFC 7761 is an Internet Standard (STD 83) and obsoletes RFC 4601. It has been updated by RFC 8736 and RFC 9436.

sections.title: What PIM-SM Is
sections.content:
Protocol Independent Multicast - Sparse Mode (PIM-SM) is a protocol for efficiently routing multicast groups that may span wide-area and inter-domain internets. It is called protocol independent because it may use the underlying unicast routing to provide reverse-path information for multicast tree building, but it does not depend on any particular unicast routing protocol.

PIM-SM version 2 was first specified in RFC 4601 as a Proposed Standard. RFC 7761 specifies the same protocol, addresses the reported errata, and removes the optional (*,*,RP) state, the PIM Multicast Border Router (PMBR) features and authentication using IPsec, because they lacked sufficient implementation and deployment experience (Appendix A, citing a survey in RFC 7063). Implementations of RFC 7761 are expected to interoperate with implementations of RFC 4601. With this document, PIM-SM advances to Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: PIM-SM is the protocol routers use so that one sender can reach many receivers without either side knowing about the other in advance. This document is the revised Internet Standard version of that protocol.

sections.title: Key Terms and State
sections.content:
The RFC defines a handful of terms the rest of the document relies on.

  • The Rendezvous Point (RP) is the router configured as the root of the non-source-specific distribution tree for a group. Joins from receivers go towards it, and data from senders goes to it, so receivers can discover the senders.
  • The Designated Router (DR) is the single router elected on each interface that acts on behalf of directly connected hosts.
  • The MRIB (Multicast Routing Information Base) is the multicast topology table, typically derived from the unicast routing table or from a protocol such as MBGP that carries multicast topology. It decides where Join and Prune messages are sent, and it provides routing metrics used in Assert messages.
  • The RPF neighbor is the neighbor the MRIB says should be used to reach an address. RPF stands for Reverse Path Forwarding: data flows along the reverse path of the Join messages.
  • The TIB (Tree Information Base) is the state created by Join/Prune messages, Assert messages and IGMP or MLD information from local hosts. A real router builds an efficient forwarding table (MFIB) from it.

TIB state comes in three kinds: (*,G) state maintains the shared tree for group G, (S,G) state maintains a source-specific tree, and (S,G,rpt) state maintains source-specific information about source S on the shared tree, such as a prune that stops S's traffic on the shared tree. This is an abstract definition: an implementation may store the state in any way that produces the same externally visible behavior.
sections.plainLanguage: The RP is the agreed meeting point for a group. The DR is the one router on a network that speaks for the local hosts. The MRIB is the topology table that tells a router which neighbor to send Join messages to.

sections.title: The Three Phases of Building a Tree
sections.content:
Senders and receivers can come and go at any time, so all three phases below may be happening at once.

Phase one: the RP tree. A receiver expresses interest in a group, typically using IGMP or MLD. Its DR sends a (*,G) Join towards the RP. The Join travels hop by hop, and each router it passes creates tree state for group G, until it reaches the RP or a router that already has that state. Together the Joins form the RP tree, also called the shared tree, because it is shared by all sources sending to the group. Joins are resent periodically, and when all receivers on a leaf network have left, the DR sends a (*,G) Prune towards the RP. A sender simply starts sending: its DR unicast-encapsulates the packets in Register messages and sends them to the RP, which decapsulates them and forwards them onto the shared tree.

Phase two: Register-Stop. Encapsulation is expensive, and the path via the RP can be long. The RP normally responds by sending an (S,G) Join towards the source S, so packets start arriving natively as well. When that happens the RP discards the encapsulated copies and sends a Register-Stop to the source's DR, which then stops encapsulating after a suppression period.

Phase three: the shortest-path tree. A router on the receiver's LAN, typically the DR, may optionally send an (S,G) Join towards S to move to a source-specific shortest-path tree (SPT). When SPT traffic starts arriving, that router drops the copies arriving over the RP tree and sends an (S,G,rpt) Prune towards the RP, which propagates until it reaches the RP or a router that still needs the traffic for other receivers.

On multi-access LANs, two routers can join to different upstream neighbors, and duplicate copies of the traffic would appear on the LAN. PIM does not prevent such duplicate joins; instead, when routers see duplicate data packets, they elect a single forwarder using Assert messages, resolved in favor of the router with (S,G) state, or otherwise the better metric.
sections.plainLanguage: First everyone meets at a central point to find each other. Then the central point asks the sender's router to send traffic directly, and finally the receivers' routers can take the direct path to the sender instead of the detour through the meeting point.

sections.title: Hello, Register, Join/Prune and Assert
sections.content:
Hello and DR election. Routers must send Hello messages on all active PIM interfaces, including point-to-point links, to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group (224.0.0.13 for IPv4, ff02::d for IPv6). Hellos are also how options are negotiated. The DR Priority option is a 32-bit number with default value 1, and the numerically larger value wins, with the higher primary IP address breaking ties. If any neighbor on the interface did not include the option, the higher IP address wins outright. A GenID option holds a random 32-bit value regenerated each time forwarding starts or restarts on the interface, so a new GenID tells neighbors the router has rebooted and its old state should be discarded. Neighbors ignore Join/Prune and Assert messages from a router they have not yet heard a Hello from.

Register. The DR encapsulates packets from local sources to the RP until it receives a Register-Stop. It then starts a Register-Stop Timer; just before the timer expires it sends a Null-Register to let the RP refresh the Register-Stop. If the timer actually expires, the DR resumes encapsulating. The DR MUST NOT register-encapsulate a packet unless its source address is a legal address for the subnet on which the packet was received.

Join/Prune. Join/Prune messages are sent towards the upstream neighbor to build and tear down shared and source trees. The RFC defines state machines for the downstream and upstream sides of each of the (*,G), (S,G) and (S,G,rpt) kinds of state, with periodic refresh and triggered messages.

Assert. When a router receives a data packet on an interface where it would normally forward that packet, it may send an Assert. The problem is resolved in favor of the upstream router with (S,G) state; if neither or both have it, the better metric towards the RP (for shared-tree traffic) or towards the source (for source-specific traffic) wins. Downstream routers then send their Joins to the Assert winner.

Switching to the SPT. Whether a last-hop router switches is decided by the policy function SwitchToSptDesired(S,G), which the implementation defines. An infinite-threshold policy never switches; a switch-on-first-packet policy switches as soon as one packet has been received.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers announce themselves with Hello messages and elect one DR per interface. They ask for traffic with Join messages and withdraw the request with Prune messages. When two routers on the same LAN both forward the same stream, Assert messages decide which one keeps forwarding.

sections.title: Finding the Rendezvous Point
sections.content:
Every PIM router in a domain must map a given group to the same RP; if they do not, black holes can appear where some receivers cannot receive some groups. The RFC does not mandate a single mechanism. It lists four, each with drawbacks: static configuration, which every PIM router MUST support; Embedded-RP, where the RP address is encoded in the IPv6 multicast group address (RFC 3956); Auto-RP, which the RFC notes has no standard specification; and the Bootstrap Router (BSR) mechanism (RFC 5059).

With the BSR mechanism, one router in each PIM domain is elected BSR through a simple election. Candidate RPs periodically unicast their candidacy to the BSR, which picks an RP-set and announces it in Bootstrap messages flooded hop by hop throughout the domain. A router maps a group address to an RP by hashing the group into the RP-set with an order-preserving hash function, one that minimizes changes if the RP-set changes; the highest hash value wins, with the highest IP address breaking ties.

The RFC also requires that any RP address that is configured, learned or advertised be reachable from all routers in the PIM domain.
sections.plainLanguage: All routers in a domain must agree on which RP a group uses, or some receivers will get nothing. That agreement can be written by hand, encoded in the group address itself, or announced by an elected bootstrap router that floods the list to everyone.

sections.title: PIM Packet Formats
sections.content:
All PIM control messages use IP protocol number 103. Some are unicast, such as Register (to the RP) and Register-Stop (back to the source of a Register). Others are multicast with TTL 1 to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group, such as Join/Prune, Assert, Hello and Bootstrap; their source address is the link-local address of the sending interface. Every message starts with a common 4-byte header: the PIM version (2), the message type, a reserved byte set to zero, and a 16-bit checksum. A message with an unrecognized version or type, or sent to the wrong kind of destination, MUST be discarded.

The checksum is a standard IP checksum over the whole PIM message, excluding the multicast data packet section of a Register; for IPv6 it also includes the IPv6 pseudo-header, with Next Header value 103. A Hello message carries options such as the Holdtime, in seconds: a Holdtime of 0xffff means the sender never times the neighbor out, and a Holdtime of zero is a goodbye that tells receivers to drop the neighbor immediately.

A Register message has a Border bit (deprecated here: set to 0 and ignored on receipt), a Null-Register bit and a reserved bit, followed by the original multicast data packet. A Join/Prune message names an upstream neighbor, a holdtime, and for each group a list of joined and pruned sources. An Assert carries a group, a source, a Metric Preference and a Metric, plus an R bit that is 1 for (*,G) Asserts and 0 for (S,G) Asserts.
sections.plainLanguage: Every PIM message begins with the same 4-byte label saying which kind it is, and then the fields specific to that kind follow. Some messages travel only to direct neighbors; others travel across the network as ordinary unicast packets.

sections.title: Source-Specific Multicast
sections.content:
The Source-Specific Multicast (SSM) service model (RFC 4607) can be implemented with a strict subset of the PIM-SM mechanisms. It uses a reserved range of group addresses, currently 232.0.0.0/8 in IPv4 and ff3x::/32 in IPv6, and the group address alone decides whether SSM or ordinary multicast semantics apply, in both data packets and PIM messages.

For a group in the SSM range, a router MUST NOT send (*,G) or (S,G,rpt) Join/Prune messages, MUST NOT send Register messages, and MUST NOT forward packets based on (*,G) or (S,G,rpt) state. A router acting as an RP MUST NOT forward Register-encapsulated packets with an SSM destination and SHOULD answer them with a Register-Stop. These rules deal with SSM-unaware legacy routers that may still send such messages.

An implementer may build a PIM-SSM-only router. It must implement the upstream and downstream (S,G) state machines, the (S,G) Assert state machine, Hello messages, neighbor discovery and DR election, and the packet forwarding rules. It does not need the Register state machine, the (*,G) and (S,G,rpt) state machines, Bootstrap RP election, the Keepalive Timer or the SPTbit: for an SSM address the Keepalive Timer is treated as always running and the SPTbit as always set.
sections.plainLanguage: In source-specific mode a receiver names the exact sender it wants, so no shared tree or meeting point is needed. Routers can therefore implement only the simpler part of PIM-SM and skip the RP machinery entirely.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
PIM relies on an MRIB populated outside of PIM, so the RFC recommends securing the sources of change to the MRIB. It then separates two kinds of forged messages.

Link-local messages (Join/Prune, Hello, Assert) are sent to the ALL-PIM-ROUTERS group and are not forwarded by a compliant router, so a forged one can only reach a LAN from a local host or from a compromised or non-compliant router. A forged Join/Prune can cause traffic to be delivered to links with no legitimate requesters, wasting bandwidth. A forged Hello can make an unauthorized router the DR, giving it control of forwarding and registration for the LAN. A forged Assert on a multi-access LAN can make the legitimate designated forwarder stop forwarding, cutting off downstream hosts.

Register and Register-Stop messages travel by normal IP forwarding, so an attacker anywhere in the network may be able to forge them. A forged Register can make the RP inject forged traffic onto the shared tree, and a forged Register-Stop can prevent a legitimate DR from registering packets, stopping local hosts from sending. These attacks do not apply to PIM-SSM-only implementations.

A router SHOULD offer an option to limit which neighbors it accepts Join/Prune, Assert and Hello messages from, by static configuration or an IPsec security association, and SHOULD NOT accept protocol messages from a router it has not heard a valid Hello from. Authentication of link-local messages is specified in RFC 5796. Denial-of-service attacks remain possible, for example by sending packets to many group addresses quickly or by forging large numbers of Joins, which consume router resources.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers mostly trust the messages they hear from neighbors. A device on the same network could forge those messages to steal the forwarding role or waste bandwidth, so the RFC suggests listening only to known neighbors and checking that senders use proper addresses. Authentication is defined in a separate document.
